working: Put \(p = dy/dx\). Then \(\sqrt{p} = 4p + 7x\); squaring gives \(p = (4p+7x)^2 = 16p^2 + 56px + 49x^2\), a rational-integral equation in \(p\). Highest derivative is the first, so order 1; the highest power of \(dy/dx\) after rationalising radicals is 2, so degree 2.

working: \(y = e^{x}(A\cos x + B\sin x)\) is the general solution of a linear ODE with roots \(1 \pm i\), i.e. \((D-1)^2 + 1 = 0 \Rightarrow D^2 - 2D + 2 = 0\), so \(y'' - 2y' + 2y = 0\), i.e. \(y'' = 2y' - 2y\). Numeric check with \(A=1, B=0\): \(y = e^x\cos x\), \(y' = e^x(\cos x - \sin x)\), \(y'' = -2e^x\sin x\); then \(2y' - 2y = -2e^x\sin x = y''\).

working: Separating, \(\mathrm{cosec}^2 y\,dy = -dx\), so \(-\cot y = -x + c_1\), i.e. \(x = \cot y + c\). Verification by implicit differentiation of (C): \(1 = -\mathrm{cosec}^2 y \cdot dy/dx \Rightarrow dy/dx = -\sin^2 y\), so \(dy/dx + \sin^2 y = 0\) exactly.

working: \(dy/dx = y(x+1)/[x(y+1)]\) separates as \(\frac{y+1}{y}dy = \frac{x+1}{x}dx\), giving \(y + \ln y = x + \ln x + c\), so \(\ln(y/x) = x - y + c\) and \(y = A x e^{x-y}\). Check: implicitly differentiating \(\ln y - \ln x = x - y + c\) gives \(y'/y - 1/x = 1 - y'\), so \(y'(1+y)/y = (x+1)/x\), i.e. \(y' = y(x+1)/[x(y+1)]\).

working: Separating, \(\tan y\,dy = \cot x\,dx\), so \(-\ln|\cos y| = \ln|\sin x| + c_1\), giving \(\sin x \cos y = c\), i.e. \(\sin x = c\sec y\). Check: differentiating \(\sin x = c\sec y\) gives \(\cos x = c\sec y\tan y\cdot y'\); since \(c\sec y = \sin x\), \(y' = \cos x/(\sin x\tan y) = \cot x\cot y\).

working: Let \(\theta = \sin^{-1}x \in [-\pi/2, \pi/2]\). \(\tan^2\theta > 1 \iff |\tan\theta| > 1 \iff \theta \in (-\pi/2, -\pi/4) \cup (\pi/4, \pi/2)\) (the endpoints \(\pm\pi/2\) are excluded because \(\tan\) is undefined there, and \(\pm\pi/4\) give \(\tan^2 = 1\), not \(>1\)). working: By the sine rule \(a = k\sin A\), \(b = k\sin B\), \(c = k\sin C\). The given equalities become \(\tan A = \tan B = \tan C\); since all angles lie in \((0,\pi)\) where \(\tan\) is injective on each branch and \(A+B+C = \pi\), we get \(A = B = C = 60^\circ\). Hence equilateral. Check: for \(a=b=c\) and \(A=B=C=60^\circ\), \(a/\cos A = a/0.5\) is common ✓.

working: Observer's eye is at height 30 m, the same level as the flag top; let \(d\) be the horizontal distance. Depression angles: to the flag foot (building top, 25 m) \(\alpha\) with \(\tan\alpha = 5/d\); to the building foot (0 m) \(\beta\) with \(\tan\beta = 30/d\). Flag subtends \(\alpha\), building subtends \(\beta - \alpha\); equating gives \(\beta = 2\alpha\). So \(30/d = \frac{2(5/d)}{1 - 25/d^2} = \frac{10d}{d^2-25}\), hence \(30(d^2-25) = 10d^2 \Rightarrow 20d^2 = 750 \Rightarrow d^2 = 37.5 = 75/2\), \(d = 5\sqrt{3/2}\). Because the flag top is level with the observer, the distance to it equals \(d\). Check: \(d = 6.1237\), \(\alpha = \arctan(0.8165) = 39.232^\circ\), \(\beta = \arctan(4.899) = 78.463^\circ = 2\alpha\) ✓.

The mathematics is unaffected: the observer's eye is level with the flag top, which is what makes the answer the plain horizontal distance.

working: Prior: \(P(\text{lost heart}) = 1/4\), \(P(\text{lost non-heart}) = 3/4\). Given a heart lost, the 51 remaining hold 12 hearts: \(P(2\text{ hearts}) = \binom{12}{2}/\binom{51}{2} = 66/1275\). Given a non-heart lost, 13 hearts remain: \(78/1275\). Bayes: \(\frac{(1/4)(66)}{(1/4)(66)+(3/4)(78)} = \frac{66}{66+234} = \frac{66}{300} = \frac{11}{50}\).
